title: Anger that won't leave
tomorrow: nobody from the masjid came. should she stop going?

cards: Two days later, still drafting the comeback in the shower. Still replaying what she said, in that tone, to someone you love. Anger that won't leave doesn't feel like a choice; it feels like weather.
There's a hadith with a strange prescription for it. Not a comeback, not a long talk, not counting to ten. Water.
Specifically wudu, the washing Muslims do before prayer. Why would washing your face have anything to do with a fight?

teach.h: FIRE IS PUT OUT WITH WATER.
teach.b: The hadith, in Abu Dawud, gives its own reason, like a little chain. Anger comes from Shaytan. Shaytan was created from fire.
Fire is put out with water. So when one of you is angry, make wudu. Some scholars grade this report's chain as weak, but the picture it draws has company.
The same collection has another: if you're standing when anger comes, sit down; if it still doesn't leave, lie down.
And in Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ says the strong one isn't the one who throws others in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when angry. Put them together and the puzzle solves itself.
None of these argue with the anger.

teach.h: CHANGE THE BODY IT LIVES IN.
teach.b: They change the body it lives in.
Wudu is slow on purpose: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet, cold water at each step. By the end, the moment has moved. Sitting lowers you; lying down lowers you more.
The Qur'an praises "those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." Control first. Forgiving can come after, when the fire is out.

how: When angry, some Muslims make wudu, sit or lie down, and say a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim, following hadith that teach changing one's state and controlling oneself in anger.

games.q: what does “anger that won't leave” mean?
o: anger you must let out or it will make you ill
anger that lingers, cooled with water and stillness
anger that proves you were right to be hurt

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: what anger comes from, in the hadith

s: the hadith says feeling anger is itself a sin
it says what to do with it: water, sitting, control.
one hadith says if you're standing when angry, sit; if it stays, lie down
change the body, and the anger has less to stand on.
the strong one, the Prophet said, is the one who wins the fight
the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry.

games.q: in the family group chat, a cousin posts something cruel about your mom. your thumbs are already typing. what does the hadith suggest first?
o: put the phone down and change your state: sit, or go wash with water.
reply right away, so the cruelty doesn't stand unanswered.
type the whole reply now but save it as a version for tomorrow.
games.why: the hadith doesn't argue with the anger; it changes the body it lives in. replying can come later, cooler, if at all.

practice: If there's water nearby, wash your hands slowly, then your face, and notice the cold. If not, take a sip of water and hold it a moment before you swallow.
Then sit back down, a little lower than before if you can, and let the rest of the sit cool whatever is still burning.

wordCard.voice: Anger that won't leave: fire, in the hadith's picture. Water, a lower posture and self-control are how it cools.

orig.note: Arabic: the washing before prayer; in this hadith, water for the fire of anger.

carryVoice: Keep this one: cool it with water, then sit down and let it pass. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 4784 (anger is from Shaytan, created from fire; fire is put out with water; so make wudu)
Sunan Abi Dawud 4782 (if angry while standing, sit; if it doesn't leave, lie down)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6114 (the strong is not the good wrestler but the one who controls himself in anger)

sources.q: those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind
